title: Threatening with death
hookLine: if people don't fear death, why threaten them with it? (Tao Te Ching 74)

cards: If you do that one more time, there will be consequences. It gets said in kitchens, offices and classrooms. Sometimes it works.
Often it buys a few hours. And sometimes it gets the reply nobody wants: go ahead. Then the threat is spent, with nothing left behind it.
Chapter seventy-four of the Tao Te Ching takes that moment as far as it goes, to the threat of death itself.

teach.b: First, the question. If the people don't fear death, the chapter asks, what's the use of threatening them with death?

It's addressed to rulers, and it's blunt logic: a threat only works on someone who still has something to lose. Push people far enough, and the biggest threat there is stops meaning anything. Second, the other side.
Suppose people always feared death, and someone did something monstrous and could be seized and put to death. Who then would dare?
It's not a call for more punishment; it shows how thin the whole strategy is. Third, the carpenter. There is, the chapter says, an executioner who does the killing, an office that belongs to it.
Killing in that executioner's place is like cutting wood in place of the master carpenter, and whoever does that rarely gets away without hurting their own hand.

Readers differ on who the executioner is: some say heaven, or the Tao itself; some say the proper course of things. Either way, reaching for the ultimate power over another person wounds the one who reaches.
Fourth, the smaller blades. Anyone can hold them: do this or I'll leave; do this or you're off the team.
The question still works at that size: what happens when the threat stops scaring them, and what does wielding it do to your own hand?
And if threats at home ever leave you afraid for your safety, you don't have to carry it alone: call local emergency help, or in the US, call or text 988.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-four as a challenge to rule by fear: threats lose their force once people stop fearing them, and taking ultimate power into one's own hands harms the one who does it.

o: an old law that every thief must be put to death
a threat that fails once people no longer fear death
a curse spoken against an enemy before a battle

p: the one whose office it is

s: chapter seventy-four argues for harsher punishment
it asks what use a death threat is when people don't fear death, and warns against taking the executioner's place.
the chapter compares killing in the executioner's place to cutting wood for the master carpenter
and whoever does that rarely escapes without hurting their own hand.
readers all agree who the executioner in chapter seventy-four is
some say heaven or the Tao; some say the proper course of things.

games.q: you rule, and the people no longer fear death. what does chapter seventy-four ask?
o: how can I make them fear it again?
what use is threatening them with death?
games.why: the chapter asks what use the threat is at all, then warns that whoever cuts in the master carpenter's place hurts their own hand.

practice: Think of one if-you-don't-then line you've used lately, out loud or only in your head, with someone else or with yourself.
Hear it once more, then notice the hand that holds it, the tight jaw, the shoulders, and imagine setting it down. What could you say instead that asks, rather than warns?

wordCard.voice: Threatening with death. Chapter seventy-four: if people don't fear death, why threaten them with it? Whoever cuts in the master carpenter's place hurts their own hand. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: the people do not fear death, the opening of chapter seventy-four.

carryVoice: Your line: no threats. A plain request asks; a threat only warns. See you tomorrow.
